title: Cisco Slashes 4,000 Jobs to Bet Big on AI, Even as Revenue Hits Record $15.8 Billion

body:
Cisco Systems announced it will cut roughly 4,000 jobs — about 5% of its global workforce — as the networking giant redirects resources toward artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and silicon development. The layoffs come despite the company posting record third-quarter revenue of $15.84 billion, a 12% year-on-year increase, and net income of $3.4 billion.

CEO Chuck Robbins framed the cuts as a strategic pivot rather than a sign of distress. Cisco raised its full-year AI infrastructure order forecast to $9 billion, with AI networking orders surging more than 50% in the quarter. The company is doubling down on four pillars: custom silicon, optics, security, and internal AI enablement for its remaining workforce. Affected employees will receive severance, pro-rated bonuses, and one year of free access to Cisco U training and certifications.

Wall Street responded enthusiastically — Cisco shares jumped as much as 18% following the announcement, as investors bet the restructuring will improve margins and position the company at the centre of the enterprise AI infrastructure buildout.

For Indian Americans in tech, the news carries a particular sting. Cisco has long been one of the largest employers of Indian-origin engineers and managers in Silicon Valley and beyond. The company's San Jose headquarters sits at the heart of a region where Indians make up a disproportionate share of the H-1B visa workforce. While Cisco has not disclosed the geographic or demographic breakdown of the layoffs, past rounds of tech layoffs have hit visa-dependent workers especially hard, as they face tight timelines to find new sponsoring employers or risk losing their immigration status.

The broader pattern is unmistakable: tech giants from Google to Meta to Microsoft have all trimmed headcount over the past two years while pouring billions into AI. For Indian tech workers — both in the US and in Cisco's substantial India operations — the message is clear: the skills that got you hired may not be the skills that keep you employed. Upskilling in AI, cloud security, and infrastructure automation is no longer optional.
author: Diaspora Desk
